14B01311: International visitors have returned to the Western Cape in record numbers since the pandemic. About 1.57 million arrived through Cape Town International in FY25/26, 35% more than in FY19/20. The recovery is therefore complete and the focus has shifted to Growth. This plan sets a target of 2.5 million international arrivals by 2035. Reaching it depends on all three goals: reshaping demand so that interest converts into visits, transforming supply so that seats, reach and product can carry the growth and building the enabling capability that sustains both. The key constraints are conversion and seat capacity at the summer peak.
37A136E5: The Western Cape does not lack interest. Conversion, seats at the summer peak and reach beyond the Metro hold it back. Reaching 2.5 million arrivals by 2035 depends on conversion work that starts in 2027, on seats held on the full routes until the runway brings relief and on the shared decisions, capital and data that sustain both. Most of the first two years' work sits inside Wesgro's mandate, the rest starts with alignment and requires concerted coordination and collaboration through the period..
732A8E88: Wesgro commissioned this study to establish a viable growth target for international arrivals to 2035 and to set out the action plan to reach it. The evidence sets the target at 2.5 million arrivals by 2035. Reaching it depends on action across demand, supply and enablement. The key constraints are the conversion of interest into visits and seat capacity at the summer peak.[^1]
0FC1C520: The chapter opens with the system at a glance. Five parts build the case for the recommendations in Chapter 3. Section 2.1 sets out why the step from recovery to growth turns on conversion and on seats at the peak. Section 2.2 draws lessons from comparator destinations. Sections 2.3, 2.4 and 2.5 then examine demand, supply and the enabling environment, on which Goals 1, 2 and 3 rest.
59FA2459: This answers the question the report began with (section 1.1). Growth to 2.5 million rests on all three goals: demand that converts, supply that can carry and deliver it and the enabling capability that sustains both. Conversion and seat capacity at the peak are the constraints that bind first. The base case holds if current marketing continues and the hub carriers keep adding capacity. The target also needs direct India and China routes, dedicated activation and national escalation. Without confirmed routes, growth reverts to the base case.
560EEDA1: The premium rests on a few mature markets, the peak season and the Cape Town Metro. Five markets supply 63% of overseas arrivals. The UK, Germany and the USA alone account for 52%. October to March carries ~62% of overseas visitor travel and the Cape Metro holds 40% of the province's 50,332 tourism assets.
270298CD: International visitors have returned to the Western Cape in record numbers, yet the system that carried the recovery rests on a few mature markets, the peak season and the Cape Town Metro.
5339A390: The premium rests on a few mature markets, the peak season, one gateway and the Cape Town Metro.
17B42456: None of these features is a shortage of interest in the province. Interest is not what holds it back; converting it is. About one in seventy interested high-value travellers arrives and six barriers stand between interest and a visit. Seats pace growth at the summer peak. A few mature markets and the peak season carry most overseas visits. Beyond the Metro, visitors who will not drive find little they can reach. In townships and rural settlements the missing piece is a local seller. The institutions that should hold the system together have thinned.
4DDB063F: Interest in the Western Cape is broad, and converting it into visits is the first task. The demand that does arrive is concentrated in a few mature markets and the peak season. The growth markets fly in through Gulf and African hubs and decide on platforms where the province is hard to find [[QUERY Q4: which markets are the growth markets?]].
0626DEBE: The peak season, October to March, carries between 61% and 62% of overseas visitors' travel in the two years for which month of travel is recorded.
6D96A107: Conversion and seat retention must move first since every other lever runs through them. Phase 1, Activate, runs from 2027 to 2028. By mid-2027 the stakeholder agreements for each initiative, a formal Unlocking Tourism Growth Steerco, a first national escalation agenda and an agreed data-sharing protocol are in place. Phase 2, Expand, runs from 2029 to 2031 and scales what the first phase proved. Phase 3, Sustain, runs from 2032 to 2035. Direct route cases go to carriers as the international terminal (about 2032) and the realigned runway (about 2033) add capacity.
693DCFF8: Phase 1 works on the levers that move before the airport can, inside existing mandates and budgets. Stakeholder agreements on roles and accountabilities are in place for each initiative in 2027 (section 4.4). Conversion work starts at once: dated reasons to travel, safety reassurance, regional information on each market's platforms and the green-season calendar (I1, I2, I3). The Cape Town Air Access partnership is re-termed to hold and add seats on the full routes and to open new routes outside the peak hours (I6). The I3 audit follows regional product from discovery to sale and prepares a bounded support trial, and two or three inclusion pilots start (I12). Steerco, the data-sharing protocol and the escalation agenda start in the first quarter (I15, I16, I17), because every other initiative reports through them.
3E05BFFC: Phase 1 also carries the tests the 2026 evidence calls for. Correlated hub-closure scenarios are complete (I6). Two flow pilots run, at Boulders and one other constrained site, in summer 2027/28 at the earliest (I11). One referral pathway across the safety services is agreed and its handoffs tested. The visa ask is rebuilt on ETA performance (I17). Accessible journeys are tested end to end before they are sold (I10). LTO services move onto lawful procurement, on a provincial practice note (I12).
54AEAF81: The research architecture comprises connected workstreams supported by a shared mandate and a current-state baseline. The study ran in four phases from November 2025 to November 2026: inception, demand-side analysis, supply-side analysis and enablement with final reporting. The evidence is integrated by theme rather than treated as a set of isolated studies. Table 1.1 lists the workstreams and Figure 1.1 shows how they relate.[^13]

22BFA5FA: Decision gates close the first two phases: Gate 1 at the end of 2028 and Gate 2 at the end of 2031. 34C853C6: The two share a focus on air access, source-market diversification, stronger tourism offerings, economic intelligence and collaboration between government and business. Both tie growth to investment, inclusion, sustainability and working infrastructure. G4J's call for tourism plans, country strategies and coordinated promotion gives this plan its policy foundation. Its emphasis on Wesgro's leadership and on cooperation across government supports the proposed delivery approach.[^9]
1159A7F9: Domestic tourism is the larger market by trips. In 2025 South Africans made about 4 million overnight trips in the Western Cape, 15.4% more than in 2024. They spent 14.3 million bed nights there at an average stay of 3.6 nights. Holidays accounted for about 1.6 million trips and visits to friends and relatives for 1.5 million. The 2024 count of 3.458 million trips was 6.1% below the start of 2020. Provinces such as the Eastern Cape drew more of the budget-conscious recovery.[^11]
45B0F3DE: This study's mandate is international and domestic channels already exist. Wesgro's With Love from the Locals campaign and Cape Town Tourism's My Cape Town campaign carry regional and local content. DEDAT's 2026/27 Annual Performance Plan places domestic marketing with the provincial tourism agencies. The plan's target, growth scenarios and indicators are built on international arrivals. Domestic tourism matters to that case as a source of green-season and regional demand and as a market that rising peak prices could crowd out. The report therefore tracks domestic trips and spend as context (Chapter 5) and leaves a domestic strategy to Wesgro and DEDAT.
